stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar in a metropolitan tertiary emergency department. Security calls you to a cubicle where a 32 year old man is shouting, pacing and punching a wall. He is intermittently accusing staff of poisoning him. He was brought in by police one hour ago after neighbours reported him yelling in the street. Collateral from a mental health team suggests he has a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder and self ceased his risperidone depot two months ago.

He refuses oral medication when offered. He does not have IV access and is not tolerating any handling. Verbal de-escalation by an experienced clinician has continued for 20 minutes without effect and he is now attempting to leave the department against advice. He is placed under the state mental health act for assessment. He has no known medical comorbidities, no known allergies and no bracelet identifying epilepsy. He is not on regular medication currently.

A five person team is available to safely administer IM medication. Cardiac monitoring is available and resuscitation equipment is at hand.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 152/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Agitated, no ataxia, no dilated pupils, no injection marks, no odour of alcohol, tremor absent
data_table.Investigations: Not yet obtained; POC glucose 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological management now?

options.text: Intramuscular promethazine 50 mg alone by the assisted team with post medication monitoring on floor
options.rationale: Promethazine as a single agent has a slow onset and unreliable sedation for acute behavioural disturbance and is not recommended as first line rapid tranquillisation. (Source: eTG: Acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with intramuscular lorazepam 2 mg given now by the assisted team
options.rationale: Haloperidol has a longer onset and higher rate of dystonia and QT prolongation compared with droperidol in AU emergency series; droperidol is preferred for rapid tranquillisation in AU emergency departments. (Source: eTG: Acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Oral olanzapine wafer 10 mg only, offered once again in the cubicle after further verbal de escalation
options.rationale: Oral medication is not appropriate when the patient has refused it and is actively attempting to leave and putting staff at risk; parenteral route is required for severe acute behavioural disturbance in this scenario. (Source: eTG: Acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Intramuscular ketamine 4 mg/kg given by the assisted five person team with continuous monitoring
options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved for extreme acute behavioural disturbance not controlled by standard combinations and requires close monitoring for airway compromise and delayed emergence; it is not first line. (Source: eTG: Acute behavioural disturbance)

options.text: Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg with intramuscular midazolam 5 mg given by the security assisted team
options.rationale: AU ED consensus for severe acute behavioural disturbance in a young adult without known cardiac disease combines IM droperidol 10 mg with IM midazolam 5-10 mg, giving faster and more predictable sedation than either alone with a good safety profile in AU emergency populations. (Source: eTG: Acute behavioural disturbance; Isbister DORM trials)

explanation.summary: Rapid tranquillisation for severe acute behavioural disturbance in AU emergency departments combines a parenteral antipsychotic and a parenteral benzodiazepine. Droperidol 10 mg IM (or IV if access) plus midazolam 5-10 mg IM has been shown effective and safe in the DORM trials by Isbister. Alternatives include olanzapine 10 mg IM or ketamine for refractory cases. Continuous monitoring of airway, respiratory rate, saturation, blood pressure and level of consciousness is essential after any parenteral sedation. Verbal de-escalation, environmental measures and offered oral therapy are always tried first.
key_points: First line severe ABD: droperidol 10 mg IM plus midazolam 5-10 mg IM
Older concerns about droperidol QT are not borne out in AU emergency data
Continuous monitoring after parenteral sedation is essential
Ketamine is reserved for extreme refractory acute behavioural disturbance
explanation.pearls: Post medication monitoring should include sedation scale (Sedation Assessment Tool used in the DORM trials), pulse oximetry, blood pressure and respiratory rate every 15 minutes for at least the first hour.

stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar seeing a 26 year old woman brought in by ambulance one hour after an impulsive ingestion of about 40 tablets of her flatmate's amitriptyline 50 mg during an argument. She has since become drowsy in the ambulance and had one witnessed seizure lasting 60 seconds that self terminated. She has taken no other medications and has no known chronic illness.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable to voice, GCS 12. Pupils are 6 mm and sluggish. Skin is dry and flushed. She is warm to touch. Bowel sounds are absent. There is no external evidence of trauma. Intravenous access has been secured and 1 L of 0.9% saline is running slowly.

Electrocardiogram taken in the ambulance and repeated on arrival shows sinus tachycardia at 128, QRS 148 ms (previously baseline 84 in old records), a prominent R wave in aVR of 4 mm, and QTc 480 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 12, dilated pupils 6 mm sluggish, dry flushed skin, absent bowel sounds, no chest signs
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 148 ms, prominent R wave aVR 4 mm, QTc 480 ms; venous pH 7.28, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, POC glucose 5.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg for the wide complex tachycardia visible on the arrival electrocardiogram
options.rationale: Amiodarone and other class I and III antiarrhythmics prolong the QT and worsen sodium channel blockade in TCA toxicity; they are contraindicated. Sodium bicarbonate is the specific treatment. (Source: eTG: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg followed by naloxone 0.4 mg with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Neither flumazenil nor naloxone address TCA toxicity; flumazenil in a mixed overdose can precipitate seizures and is contraindicated when TCA is possible. (Source: eTG: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg for seizure prophylaxis after the witnessed seizure in the ambulance
options.rationale: Phenytoin is a class Ib antiarrhythmic that can worsen the sodium channel blockade caused by TCAs; benzodiazepines are the first line for TCA related seizures if they recur. (Source: eTG: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g orally alone via a nasogastric tube with continuous cardiac monitoring alone
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is contraindicated in a drowsy patient with an unprotected airway due to aspiration risk, and does not address the sodium channel blockade already manifest on ECG. (Source: eTG: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol bolus over 5 minutes, repeat guided by QRS width and blood pressure
options.rationale: TCA sodium channel blockade causing QRS widening over 100 ms, R wave in aVR over 3 mm and hypotension requires sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus to overcome the blockade by sodium loading and alkalinisation; further boluses are titrated to narrowing QRS and blood pressure. (Source: eTG: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning; NSW Poisons Information Centre)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes anticholinergic toxidrome plus sodium channel blockade of the cardiac fast channel, producing QRS widening, prominent R wave in aVR, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia and seizures. QRS over 100 ms and R wave in aVR over 3 mm predict cardiotoxicity and are indications for sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus (typical 100 mmol) titrated to narrowing QRS and pH 7.45-7.55. Seizures are treated with benzodiazepines. Class I and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Flumazenil is contraindicated when TCA is possible.
key_points: TCA cardiotoxicity: QRS over 100 ms, R in aVR over 3 mm, hypotension
Treatment: sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus, titrate to QRS narrowing
Benzodiazepines for seizures; avoid phenytoin
Avoid class I and III antiarrhythmics
explanation.pearls: Target pH 7.45-7.55 during bicarbonate therapy; overshooting alkalosis worsens hypokalaemia which itself prolongs QT and worsens arrhythmia risk.

stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 58 year old man in the medical outpatient clinic three months after a first unprovoked segmental pulmonary embolism. He presented then with acute pleuritic chest pain and mild hypoxia; CTPA showed a segmental left lower lobe filling defect without right heart strain and D-dimer was raised. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily and reports no bleeding or bruising and no symptoms of recurrence.

He has no known heritable thrombophilia, no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, and no active malignancy. He does not smoke, exercises three times weekly, and has a BMI of 26. Recent malignancy screen appropriate to age (bowel cancer screening, PSA discussion, chest imaging) has returned normal.

His current blood pressure is 128/78, resting pulse 68 and full blood count and renal function are within normal limits. He asks about how long he needs to remain on his anticoagulant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no calf swelling, no bleeding on inspection
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m2, ALT 24 U/L, HAS-BLED score 1 (age)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from three months onwards?

options.text: Switch to warfarin with target INR 2 to 3 for a further nine months then cease anticoagulation
options.rationale: There is no advantage of warfarin over apixaban in unprovoked PE without antiphospholipid syndrome; nine months of warfarin then cessation still stops at a point where recurrence risk remains high. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

options.text: Cease apixaban after a further three months of full dose therapy then monitor clinically at review
options.rationale: Six months of anticoagulation is only sufficient for provoked venous thromboembolism where the transient trigger has resolved; unprovoked PE has too high a recurrence rate to safely stop. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

options.text: Continue apixaban indefinitely at reduced dose 2.5 mg twice daily with annual bleeding risk review
options.rationale: Unprovoked PE has an annual recurrence risk of about 10% in the first year off anticoagulation; indefinite anticoagulation is recommended unless bleeding risk is high, and the AMPLIFY-EXT trial supports apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months with a low bleeding rate. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism; AMPLIFY-EXT NEJM 2013)

options.text: Add aspirin 100 mg daily as anticoagulation replacement and cease apixaban at the current review
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces VTE recurrence by only about 30% compared with anticoagulation and is inferior to low dose apixaban continuation; ASPIRE and WARFASA trials do not support aspirin instead of a DOAC. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

options.text: Insert an inferior vena cava filter today and cease all further anticoagulation at the review
options.rationale: IVC filters are reserved for patients with acute VTE and an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; they do not treat existing thrombus and carry their own long term complications. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

explanation.summary: Provoked VTE with a resolvable trigger is treated for 3 months. Unprovoked proximal DVT or PE has a recurrence rate of about 10% at 1 year and about 30% at 5 years off anticoagulation and is treated with indefinite anticoagulation unless bleeding risk is high. AMPLIFY-EXT showed apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond the initial 6 months of full dose was as effective as 5 mg with lower bleeding. Cancer associated VTE is treated with LMWH or edoxaban or apixaban for a minimum 6 months and often ongoing while cancer active. Antiphospholipid syndrome VTE is treated with warfarin, not a DOAC.
key_points: Provoked VTE: 3 months anticoagulation
Unprovoked proximal VTE or PE: indefinite anticoagulation unless bleeding risk high
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is the extended phase dose (AMPLIFY-EXT)
Antiphospholipid syndrome VTE: warfarin, not DOAC
explanation.pearls: Distal isolated calf DVT and subsegmental PE without symptoms have different rules and may be managed with surveillance in selected patients - a proximal or symptomatic segmental PE is not one of them.

stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 42 year old woman with two days of right sided loin pain, fever and dysuria. She reports vomiting twice this morning and cannot tolerate oral fluids. She has no history of urological surgery, renal stones or recurrent UTI. She is not pregnant and has no known drug allergies.

On examination she is warm and flushed with tender right renal angle percussion. Abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness. Chest is clear. She has no rigors currently but had one this morning.

Urinalysis: leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood 1+. Midstream urine sample sent. Blood cultures drawn from a peripheral cannula. She has not received any antibiotics in the past three months. She has no history of recent overseas travel or antibiotic resistance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, mild suprapubic tenderness, no peritonism, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cells 16.8 x10^9/L, CRP 168 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L (baseline 70), urinalysis leucocytes 3+ nitrites positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for seven days at the current outpatient dosing regimen from home
options.rationale: Trimethoprim is not first line for pyelonephritis due to rising resistance, and this woman cannot tolerate oral therapy due to vomiting; oral trimethoprim is used for simple cystitis, not pyelonephritis. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily with intravenous amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours empirically
options.rationale: eTG empirical therapy for acute pyelonephritis in an adult tolerating IV is gentamicin plus amoxicillin (or ampicillin), covering E coli and Enterococcus with excellent renal tissue penetration; oral therapy is used only for mild pyelonephritis and she is vomiting and unable to tolerate oral. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for ten days at outpatient dosing on discharge from hospital
options.rationale: Ciprofloxacin is reserved for beta lactam allergy or documented resistance in AU guidance due to fluoroquinolone associated side effects and resistance concerns; she can be given the first line IV regimen. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily as inpatient therapy
options.rationale: Vancomycin adds no useful cover for the uropathogens (E coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus) in a woman with no MRSA risk factors and no penicillin allergy; gentamicin plus amoxicillin is the AU first line. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for seven days at outpatient dosing on ward discharge
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate tissue concentrations in the kidney and is contraindicated in pyelonephritis; she also cannot tolerate oral therapy. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in an adult requiring admission is treated empirically with IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin (or ampicillin) per eTG, covering E coli and Enterococcus. Ceftriaxone 1 g daily IV is an alternative when aminoglycosides are contraindicated. Duration is 10-14 days total with switch to oral therapy guided by susceptibilities once systemically well. Ciprofloxacin is reserved for beta lactam allergy or susceptibility results. Nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim have no role in pyelonephritis. Mild pyelonephritis with tolerable oral therapy may be treated as an outpatient with amoxicillin clavulanate or cefalexin per susceptibilities.
key_points: First line IV pyelonephritis: gentamicin plus amoxicillin
Ceftriaxone alternative when aminoglycosides contraindicated
Total duration 10-14 days with early oral switch when possible
Nitrofurantoin does not treat pyelonephritis (poor tissue penetration)
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin dosing in acute settings is 5 mg/kg once daily; check gentamicin trough level at 24 h if continued beyond 48 h and reassess renal function daily.

stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34 year old man with a two day history of vomiting, polyuria and polydipsia. He has established type 1 diabetes on twice daily insulin who has been unwell with viral gastroenteritis and reduced his insulin doses. He is drowsy but orientated on arrival.

Capillary blood glucose is 26.4 mmol/L. Venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, ketones 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 100 mmol/L. Creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 78 six months ago). His weight is 78 kg. Urinalysis: ketones 3+, glucose 3+.

He has no cardiac or renal comorbidity and no chest pain. Chest x-ray is clear. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118 with peaked T waves in the precordial leads.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, capillary refill 3 s, drowsy GCS 14, Kussmaul respiration, acetone breath
data_table.Investigations: As above; POC glucose 26.4 mmol/L, venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8, ketones 5.6, sodium 132, potassium 5.6, creatinine 132

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid regimen?

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol infusion over 2 hours to correct the venous pH before insulin
options.rationale: Bicarbonate in DKA is reserved for pH under 6.9 or life threatening hyperkalaemia; giving it at pH 7.14 does not improve outcomes and can worsen intracellular acidosis and cerebral oedema. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Intravenous 5% dextrose 1 L over 1 hour to protect against hypoglycaemia during insulin infusion start
options.rationale: His glucose is 26.4 mmol/L and dextrose is not indicated as initial fluid; dextrose is added later when glucose falls to under 14 mmol/L to allow continued insulin without hypoglycaemia. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Intravenous 0.45% sodium chloride 1 L over 1 hour to avoid hyperchloraemia and correct free water deficit
options.rationale: 0.45% saline is a hypotonic maintenance fluid not indicated for initial resuscitation of DKA; rapid infusion of hypotonic fluid raises cerebral oedema risk especially in younger patients. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% saline 1 L over 1 hour, reassess potassium, then start fixed rate insulin infusion
options.rationale: AU consensus DKA pathway (RACGP, endocrine consensus) starts with 0.9% saline 1 L in the first hour to restore intravascular volume; potassium is added when serum potassium is under 5.5 and fixed rate insulin infusion started at 0.1 units/kg/hour after initial fluid. His potassium is at 5.6 so no potassium is added yet. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; ADS/ADEA position statement 2020)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L with 40 mmol/L potassium chloride over 1 hour with insulin start
options.rationale: Potassium is added only when serum potassium is under 5.5 mmol/L; giving 40 mmol potassium with his admission potassium of 5.6 mmol/L risks worsening hyperkalaemia and precipitating a cardiac arrest. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management follows a sequence of fluid, then potassium consideration, then fixed rate insulin infusion, plus glucose monitoring and dextrose addition when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L. First hour is 0.9% saline 1 L. Potassium is added at 40 mmol/L when serum potassium is under 5.5, held when 5.5 or higher. Fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour after fluid started. Ketosis clearance is the endpoint, not glucose normalisation - target beta hydroxybutyrate fall of 0.5 mmol/L/hour and bicarbonate rise of 3 mmol/L/hour. Bicarbonate is reserved for pH under 6.9.
key_points: First hour: 0.9% saline 1 L
Add 40 mmol/L potassium when K+ under 5.5
Fixed rate insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour
Add 10% dextrose when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L to allow continued insulin
explanation.pearls: Ketosis, not hyperglycaemia, is the target of DKA treatment - keep insulin running until beta hydroxybutyrate is under 0.6 mmol/L even if that requires simultaneous dextrose to prevent hypoglycaemia.

stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 46 year old man in the emergency department with 24 hours of vomiting, generalised abdominal pain and light headedness. He has Addison's disease diagnosed five years ago and takes hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking, 10 mg at midday and fludrocortisone 100 microgram in the morning. He has been unable to keep his hydrocortisone down and stopped taking any medication yesterday. He also has type 1 diabetes on insulin.

He looks unwell and clammy. His skin is hyperpigmented over the buccal mucosa and palmar creases. Cardiovascular examination reveals postural hypotension with a systolic drop from 92 lying to 68 standing before you stop the manoeuvre. Chest is clear and abdomen soft without peritonism.

Routine investigations: sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 82). A cortisol and ACTH sample has been drawn.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 84/56 mmHg lying, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.5 degC
data_table.Examination: Cool clammy skin, buccal and palmar hyperpigmentation, postural drop with symptoms, abdomen soft, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128, potassium 5.4, glucose 3.2, creatinine 128, cortisol and ACTH sent, urinalysis negative, POC beta hCG not applicable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give an oral doubled dose of hydrocortisone 40 mg now and observe him for oral tolerance on the ward
options.rationale: He is vomiting and cannot keep oral medication down; the sick day rule for oral doubling has failed and parenteral therapy is required. Oral now delays effective treatment. (Source: eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus with IV 0.9% saline 1 L over the first hour and glucose monitoring
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis in a known Addison patient with vomiting, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia; immediate management is 100 mg hydrocortisone IV bolus with rapid saline resuscitation and correction of glucose. Do not wait for cortisol result. (Source: Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guideline 2016; eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: Give dexamethasone 4 mg intravenous and await the synacthen test result before hydrocortisone bolus
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is preferred in acute adrenal crisis because it provides both glucocorticoid and some mineralocorticoid activity; awaiting synacthen results before treatment risks death. Dexamethasone can be used only if cortisol assay is pending and hydrocortisone is unavailable. (Source: Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guideline 2016)

options.text: Give intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microgram bolus and observe for haemodynamic response on the ward
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is a pure mineralocorticoid and does not provide the glucocorticoid activity urgently needed in adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone at stress doses covers both. (Source: eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: Give 3% hypertonic saline 100 mL bolus for hyponatraemia and defer steroid until sodium corrects
options.rationale: The hyponatraemia is driven by cortisol and aldosterone deficiency; hypertonic saline is not indicated as first line correction here and correcting sodium too rapidly risks osmotic demyelination without addressing the crisis. (Source: eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis when a known Addison patient presents with vomiting, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia during physiological stress. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, followed by 200 mg/24 h by continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours IV or IM, plus rapid IV saline (1-2 L in the first hour, guided by response), correction of hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose, and treatment of the precipitant. Cortisol and ACTH samples should be taken pre steroid where possible but treatment must not be delayed for the result. Patients receive a sick day management plan with parenteral hydrocortisone at home.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 200 mg/24 h infusion or 50 mg IV/IM q6h
IV saline 1-2 L first hour then guided by response
Correct hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose
Sick day rules: double dose oral if unwell, parenteral IM hydrocortisone if vomiting
explanation.pearls: Every patient with Addison's disease should carry a medic alert bracelet and a home IM hydrocortisone Act-O-Vial that they and family can use before ambulance arrival - the difference between minor illness and cardiac arrest can be one missed cover dose.

stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 58 year old woman with a two day history of fever, malaise and a painful spreading rash. She started allopurinol 300 mg for gout three weeks ago. Yesterday she noticed red patches on her chest that have progressed to blisters on her chest, back and arms overnight.

On examination she has flaccid bullae and desquamating erythematous skin covering approximately 12% of body surface area. Nikolsky sign is positive with gentle lateral pressure lifting the epidermis. Her lips are crusted and there are erosions on her buccal mucosa and conjunctivae. She reports pain on urination and inspection reveals genital mucosal erosions.

Her eGFR is 42 mL/min/1.73 m2 baseline. She takes ramipril 5 mg and metformin. She had a first episode of gout six weeks ago with three subsequent episodes prompting the allopurinol start. She is of Han Chinese ancestry but was not tested for HLA B*58:01 before allopurinol was commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Flaccid bullae with 12% BSA involvement, positive Nikolsky, mucosal involvement at lips, oral cavity, conjunctivae and genitalia
data_table.Investigations: White cells 14.2 x10^9/L, neutrophils 11.8, creatinine 148 micromol/L (baseline 118), ALT 96 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, glucose 6.4 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue allopurinol, add oral prednisolone 50 mg daily and manage in the general medical ward
options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug is contraindicated in SJS/TEN; systemic corticosteroids have inconsistent evidence and are not recommended as first line without specialist input, and a general ward cannot provide the burns level care required. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

options.text: Cease allopurinol, transfer to burns unit, calculate SCORTEN and start meticulous supportive care
options.rationale: SJS/TEN suspected by mucosal involvement at two or more sites plus epidermal detachment mandates immediate cessation of the culprit drug (allopurinol is the highest risk in AU) and transfer to a burns or high dependency unit; SCORTEN estimates mortality and drives resource allocation. Supportive care mirrors burns management. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions; ADRAC alert on allopurinol HLA B*58:01)
source_refs: ADRAC alert on allopurinol HLA B*58:01

options.text: Perform skin biopsy today and start empirical amoxicillin clavulanate 875 mg twice daily for cellulitis
options.rationale: This is not cellulitis and empirical antibiotics can worsen the reaction by introducing further culprit drugs; biopsy can be done but must not delay drug cessation and transfer to specialist care. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

options.text: Discharge home with topical steroid cream and outpatient dermatology review scheduled in one week
options.rationale: SJS/TEN mortality with TEN over 30% BSA reaches 30-50% and requires intensive supportive care; outpatient management is inconsistent with the diagnosis and puts the patient at risk of sepsis and death. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

options.text: Restart allopurinol at reduced dose 100 mg and add azathioprine as a steroid sparing agent long term
options.rationale: Rechallenge with the culprit drug in SJS/TEN is contraindicated; a lower dose is not safer, the reaction is idiosyncratic and immune mediated. Rechallenge has caused fatal recurrence. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

explanation.summary: SJS and TEN are severe cutaneous adverse reactions on a spectrum defined by percentage of body surface area with detachment (SJS under 10%, SJS-TEN overlap 10-30%, TEN over 30%). Culprit drugs in AU include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, sulphonamides and NSAIDs. Immediate management is cessation of the culprit drug, transfer to a burns or HDU for meticulous supportive care (fluid balance, temperature, wound care, ophthalmology and urology involvement), and SCORTEN prognosis calculation. Systemic corticosteroids, IVIG and ciclosporin are used in some centres but evidence is inconsistent. HLA B*58:01 screening before allopurinol is now recommended for South East Asian, Han Chinese, Korean and Thai ancestry patients due to strong association.
key_points: SJS/TEN classification: SJS under 10% BSA, overlap 10-30%, TEN over 30%
First step: cease culprit drug immediately, transfer to burns unit
Allopurinol is the highest risk AU culprit for SCAR
HLA B*58:01 screening for allopurinol in Southeast Asian and Han Chinese ancestry
explanation.pearls: SCORTEN uses 7 parameters (age, malignancy, tachycardia, BSA detached, serum urea, bicarbonate, glucose) at 24 h to estimate mortality; each point roughly doubles risk.

sources.label: ADRAC alert on allopurinol HLA B*58:01

stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 52 year old woman with a two week history of worsening bulbar and limb weakness on a background of established acetylcholine receptor antibody positive myasthenia gravis. She was diagnosed three years ago and takes pyridostigmine 60 mg four times daily and prednisolone 20 mg daily. She was started on azithromycin two days ago for a suspected chest infection by her GP.

Today she reports increasing difficulty swallowing with nasal regurgitation of liquids. Her voice has become nasal. She feels short of breath at rest. On the ward she cannot count above 15 in a single breath.

On examination she has bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion and difficulty holding her arms outstretched for 30 seconds. Chest auscultation is clear with reduced breath sounds bilaterally. Peak inspiratory pressure is -18 cmH2O and vital capacity is 12 mL/kg. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibody titre is very high.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.1 degC
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion, cannot maintain arms outstretched 30 s, count to breath 15, single breath count consistent with vital capacity 12 mL/kg
data_table.Investigations: Vital capacity 780 mL (12 mL/kg for 65 kg), NIF -18 cmH2O, arterial pH 7.36, pCO2 47 mmHg, pO2 78 mmHg, chest x-ray clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Transfer to ICU for respiratory monitoring, cease azithromycin and start plasma exchange or IVIG
options.rationale: Myasthenic crisis with vital capacity under 15 mL/kg and NIF worse than -20 cmH2O predicts imminent respiratory failure; ICU monitoring for elective intubation before decompensation is essential. Plasma exchange and IVIG are equally effective first line rescue therapies. Azithromycin and other macrolides worsen weakness in myasthenia gravis and must be ceased. (Source: RANZCP neurology practice; ANZAN myasthenia guidance; eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

options.text: Continue current pyridostigmine and increase to 90 mg six times daily with ongoing ward monitoring
options.rationale: Pyridostigmine escalation risks cholinergic crisis with similar weakness and increased secretions; higher doses do not treat the underlying immune process and delay definitive rescue therapy. (Source: eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

options.text: Administer intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 1 g and observe her on the general medical ward tonight
options.rationale: High dose steroids can transiently worsen myasthenic weakness in the first 5-10 days and must be given with rescue cover in place; ward observation without ICU monitoring risks unrecognised respiratory failure. (Source: eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

options.text: Perform an urgent oesophagoscopy today to evaluate the swallowing dysfunction before further therapy
options.rationale: The dysphagia is neuromuscular from the crisis and not structural; oesophagoscopy is not indicated and would delay life saving treatment. (Source: eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

options.text: Administer intravenous edrophonium 10 mg diagnostically before deciding on any further treatment plan
options.rationale: Edrophonium (Tensilon) was historically used diagnostically but is no longer available in AU and does not change management in a known seropositive MG patient in crisis; treatment should not be delayed. (Source: ANZAN myasthenia guidance)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is defined by neuromuscular respiratory failure requiring ventilator support or imminent respiratory failure. Precipitants include infection and specific medications (macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta blockers, magnesium). Bedside markers of imminent decompensation are vital capacity under 15 mL/kg (or 1 L) and NIF worse than -20 cmH2O; hypercapnia is a late finding. First line rescue therapies are plasma exchange or IVIG (equal efficacy), with concurrent high dose steroids introduced cautiously due to early worsening. Non invasive ventilation may buy time in selected patients; early elective intubation avoids decompensation.
key_points: Crisis markers: VC under 15 mL/kg, NIF worse than -20 cmH2O, hypercapnia is late
First line rescue: plasma exchange OR IVIG (equal efficacy)
Macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta blockers all worsen MG
Cholinergic crisis mimics MG crisis but has muscarinic features (sweating, salivation, miosis)
explanation.pearls: Early transfer to ICU for airway management prevents catastrophic respiratory arrest - a patient who cannot count to 20 in one breath should not stay on the ward.

stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar in a tertiary emergency department reviewing a 62 year old man brought in by ambulance with sudden onset tearing interscapular chest pain that started 45 minutes ago while gardening. He has a background of long standing hypertension on ramipril and amlodipine and is a current smoker.

On arrival he is diaphoretic and in severe pain (10/10). Blood pressures are 218/122 in the right arm and 178/106 in the left. Pulses are weak in the left radial and absent in the left femoral. Chest and abdominal examination is otherwise unremarkable. He is neurologically intact.

Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia at 118 without ischaemic changes. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum. Bedside troponin is not raised. A CT aortogram taken during resuscitation shows a Stanford type A dissection extending from the ascending aorta through the arch into the descending aorta and into the origin of the left common iliac artery. Cardiothoracic surgery has been called and is 20 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 218/122 mmHg (right arm) 178/106 mmHg (left arm), respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, pain 10/10, absent left femoral pulse, weak left radial, normal neurology, no aortic regurgitation murmur
data_table.Investigations: CT aortogram Stanford type A dissection, troponin negative, urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L, group and save sent, POC glucose 6.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management?

options.text: IV verapamil 5 mg for rate control targeting a heart rate under 60 before starting a vasodilator
options.rationale: Verapamil is used only when beta blockers are contraindicated; esmolol or labetalol are first line for their titratable pharmacology and preferred agents in AU practice. (Source: eTG: Aortic dissection)

options.text: IV glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg without prior beta blockade
options.rationale: Vasodilator before rate control causes reflex tachycardia and increases aortic wall shear stress, propagating the dissection; beta blockade must precede vasodilator therapy in dissection. (Source: AHA/ACC aortic dissection guideline 2022)

options.text: IV alteplase 0.9 mg/kg to lyse a suspected thrombus in the left circumflex coronary artery immediately
options.rationale: This is aortic dissection and troponin is negative; thrombolysis in aortic dissection can extend the dissection and cause fatal haemorrhage and is absolutely contraindicated. (Source: AHA/ACC aortic dissection guideline 2022)

options.text: IV fentanyl for analgesia and hold antihypertensive therapy pending immediate transfer to theatre
options.rationale: Untreated hypertension propagates the dissection and increases the risk of rupture and death during the 20 minute wait for theatre; blood pressure and heart rate control are urgent alongside analgesia. (Source: AHA/ACC aortic dissection guideline 2022)

options.text: IV esmolol infusion titrated to HR under 60 and systolic 100 to 120 before adding IV glyceryl trinitrate
options.rationale: Aortic dissection requires heart rate reduction before vasodilation to reduce dP/dt and shear stress; unopposed vasodilator causes reflex tachycardia and worsens propagation. Target heart rate under 60 and systolic 100-120 mmHg. Esmolol first, then GTN or sodium nitroprusside added. (Source: eTG: Aortic dissection; AHA/ACC aortic dissection guideline 2022)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is managed by simultaneously controlling heart rate then blood pressure to reduce dP/dt and aortic wall shear stress. First line is intravenous beta blocker (esmolol infusion, or labetalol) titrated to heart rate under 60 before adding an intravenous vasodilator (GTN or sodium nitroprusside) to bring systolic blood pressure to 100-120 mmHg. Type A dissections (ascending aorta involved) are surgical emergencies with mortality of 1-2% per hour untreated; type B dissections are usually managed medically with intervention for complications (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or hypertension). Thrombolysis is absolutely contraindicated.
key_points: Aortic dissection dP/dt reduction: rate first then vasodilator
Target: heart rate under 60, systolic 100-120 mmHg
Type A: immediate surgery. Type B: medical unless complications
Thrombolysis is absolutely contraindicated in aortic dissection
explanation.pearls: Blood pressure differential between arms of more than 20 mmHg, absent limb pulse, or new aortic regurgitation with tearing pain is dissection until proven otherwise, and time to imaging saves lives.

stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 78 year old woman brought in by ambulance with sudden onset right sided weakness and dysphasia one hour ago. She is on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, target INR 2-3. She takes no other anticoagulant or antiplatelet.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, GCS 12 (E3 V3 M6), has a dense right hemiparesis (0/5 arm, 1/5 leg) and expressive dysphasia. Vital signs show blood pressure 218/118 mmHg and heart rate 98 irregular. Non contrast CT head shows a 32 mL left basal ganglia haematoma with no intraventricular extension, midline shift 3 mm. There is no evidence of a large vessel occlusion on CT angiogram.

Urgent bloods return INR 3.4, haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. She is otherwise haemodynamically stable and there is no external bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 /min irregular, blood pressure 218/118 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: GCS 12, dense right hemiparesis, expressive dysphasia, no external bleeding, no signs of trauma
data_table.Investigations: INR 3.4, haemoglobin 128, platelets 240, creatinine 92, CT head 32 mL left basal ganglia haematoma with 3 mm midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combination of interventions in the first hour?

options.text: IV vitamin K 10 mg plus PCC 50 units/kg now, and IV labetalol titrated to systolic 130 to 140 in 1 hour
options.rationale: Warfarin associated ICH needs immediate reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate (dose by INR and weight, typically 25-50 units/kg) plus vitamin K 10 mg IV for sustained reversal; PCC works within minutes while vitamin K sustains it. INTERACT2 and ATACH-2 support rapid intensive systolic BP lowering to 130-140 mmHg within one hour, better than 180 mmHg or higher targets. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal; INTERACT2 NEJM 2013; NHFA/CSANZ acute stroke guideline)

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg without prothrombin complex concentrate and permissive hypertension
options.rationale: FFP takes hours to fully reverse warfarin and requires large volumes with fluid overload risk; PCC gives faster reversal with less volume. Permissive hypertension in ICH is inconsistent with INTERACT2 evidence for lowering to 130-140 mmHg. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal; INTERACT2 NEJM 2013)

options.text: Intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg for suspected stroke and hold blood pressure treatment pending review
options.rationale: Alteplase is absolutely contraindicated in intracerebral haemorrhage and would extend the haematoma with lethal effect; the CT already demonstrates haemorrhagic stroke. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ acute stroke guideline)

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg intravenous alone and monitor INR every 6 hours without prothrombin complex concentrate
options.rationale: Vitamin K alone takes 6-24 hours to reverse warfarin, which is too slow in the setting of an expanding intracerebral haematoma; PCC is required for immediate reversal with vitamin K as adjunct for sustained effect. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal)

options.text: Idarucizumab 5 g intravenous for anticoagulant reversal with blood pressure target 180 over 100 mmHg
options.rationale: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin; using it here provides no reversal and delays PCC administration. Systolic BP target of 180 is above INTERACT2 evidence for intensive lowering. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal)

explanation.summary: Warfarin associated intracerebral haemorrhage requires immediate reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate 25-50 units/kg (dose by INR and weight) plus IV vitamin K 10 mg. PCC restores clotting factors within minutes; vitamin K keeps INR reversed as PCC effect wanes. FFP is slower, larger volume and inferior. Intensive systolic blood pressure lowering to 130-140 mmHg within one hour (INTERACT2, ATACH-2) reduces haematoma expansion and improves functional outcome compared with a 180 mmHg target. Neurosurgical consultation is indicated for supratentorial haematomas with mass effect and cerebellar haemorrhage over 3 cm; DOAC reversal uses agent specific antidotes (idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC for factor Xa inhibitors).
key_points: Warfarin ICH: PCC 25-50 units/kg plus vitamin K 10 mg IV
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet or 4F-PCC for factor Xa DOACs
Target systolic BP 130-140 mmHg within one hour (INTERACT2, ATACH-2)
Alteplase is contraindicated in haemorrhagic stroke
explanation.pearls: PCC dose depends on both INR and weight - a common AU shortcut for high INR is 50 units/kg capped at 3000 units for adults, but the local haematology pathway should always be followed.
